take_homes: my agent file and my own rules contradicted each other and i never saw it. a pass over the files with my rules caught it, and the first generic pass got one wrong.
an injection through a document the agent reads is the real attack. the send gate and write scope decide how bad it gets.
a mitigation written as a prompt rule isn't a control. the 'i can't tell' rows and the residual get written down and owned.

monday.move: run the packaged security-audit skill over the sales-team setup before anyone touches it, and switch off send and unscoped write on anything that reads shared docs
monday.who: me, then one of the platform engineers to own it
monday.when: Monday morning, before the weekend build goes anywhere
monday.stop_condition: every 'violating' row is fixed with a permission and not a prompt, and the 'i can't tell' rows each have a named owner
monday.blocker: nobody in sales asked for it and i haven't checked who maintains it. the audit may also tell me to shelve it.

misconception.why: the raw first pass called a rule compliant and was wrong, and the injection that hit the Q2 review looked like normal content. 'looks fine' is exactly what i said in the sample line, so checking isn't just for beginners. i still skipped the grill and the pre-reads, so i'm not fully changed.

one_line: the first hour is slow if your engineers already run agents, but the audit found things i'd have shipped, so send your non-engineers through it before they build.
